planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Paradise stays smaller and more compact than most American persimmon selections, making it a reasonable fit where space is limited.

directions: Paradise traces back to a seedling James Claypool grew and numbered H-63-A in his St. Elmo, Illinois breeding rows, later renamed for its popularity among Amish growers near Paradise, Pennsylvania. The tree stays comparatively small for an American persimmon yet bears heavily, setting large fruit with clear, speck-free flesh that ripens in September and is prized for cooking down into pulp for breads and puddings. Like all American persimmon, fruit must soften fully after a frost or extended ripening before it loses its astringency. A second cultivar or seedling male nearby improves fruit set.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society (Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars, 2025)

planting.note: Plant grafted stock in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; H-120 bears at a young age and crops heavily once established.

directions: H-120 is one of the many numbered selections James Claypool pulled from his decades-long persimmon trial rows in St. Elmo, Illinois, confirmed as a distinct hexaploid clone in Kentucky State University ploidy surveys. It carries large fruit for the species, with clear, juicy pulp that stays free of the dark specking that mars lesser seedling persimmons, and it ripens earlier than many Claypool-line selections. The tree takes a rounded canopy and fruits precociously once established, tolerating the heat, drought, and poor soils typical of native persimmon growing sites. Plant with another cultivar or a male seedling nearby for reliable seed-set and heavier crops.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring; SFES belongs to the tetraploid race of American persimmon, so pair it with another tetraploid selection rather than the more common hexaploid cultivars for dependable pollination.

directions: SFES was selected from wild stock around Hopkinsville, Kentucky by grower Lucky Pittman and later confirmed by flow cytometry as one of only a handful of named American persimmon cultivars belonging to the 60-chromosome tetraploid race rather than the more common 90-chromosome hexaploid race. It carries red-skinned fruit on a notably heavy-bearing tree. Because the two persimmon races are cross-incompatible, growers should plant it alongside another tetraploid cultivar rather than a typical hexaploid selection to ensure full, well-formed fruit. Like other American persimmons, fruit needs to soften well past the first hard frost before the astringency fades.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil; its narrow, weeping habit suits it to tight planting strips where a standard full-size persimmon would not fit.

directions: Patented in 2015 (US PP25,689) by breeder Ray Jackson as 'JN5' and sold under the trade name Magic Fountain, this selection was found as a single open-pollinated seedling near Belvidere, Tennessee in 2007, chosen for its distinctly columnar trunk with strongly weeping side branches rather than the broad spreading crown typical of American persimmon. It stays compact at roughly 10-15 feet tall, making it one of the few named cultivars suited to small-space or ornamental plantings rather than orchard rows. A female clone, it sets small, rounded, golden-orange fruit in fall that needs full softening past frost to shed its astringency. Site it where the dramatic winter silhouette of its weeping branches can be appreciated as well as its fruit.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Rubescens is a pink-flowered form of apple serviceberry, the natural hybrid between A. canadensis and A. laevis, selected for deep pink buds that open to pale pink blossoms instead of the pure white typical of the cross. It keeps the same early-summer crop of sweet, blueberry-like fruit and multi-season appeal as other grandiflora cultivars, ripening to orange and red fall foliage. Its compact, upright-spreading habit works well as a small specimen tree or large shrub border planting. Grow in moist, well-drained soil; light shade is tolerated but flowering and fruit set are heaviest in full sun.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in early spring; Strata tolerates shadier sites than most serviceberry cultivars, making it a strong pick for true understory plantings.

directions: Strata was selected at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Arboretum for its distinctly horizontal, tiered branching pattern, an unusual architectural trait for Allegheny serviceberry, which typically grows as an upright multi-stemmed clump. Clouds of white flowers open in early spring, followed by blue-purple berries that are sweet enough for fresh eating if picked before birds clear the tree, and foliage turns orange in fall. It handles conditions from full sun down into full shade better than most serviceberry selections, fitting true woodland-edge and understory plantings. Give it moderate, consistent moisture and well-drained soil for the best form.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil; Spring Glory's compact size fits foundation plantings and smaller yards where full-size serviceberry species would quickly overrun the space.

directions: Spring Glory is a Proven Winners introduction selected from Canadian serviceberry for a notably compact habit, topping out around 12 feet tall and 6-8 feet wide versus the 15-25 feet typical of seedling-grown A. canadensis. It carries the same lightly fragrant white April flowers, sweet purple summer berries, and bright orange fall color as the species, just on a scale suited to smaller residential lots. Birds strip the ripe fruit quickly, so pick early if you want a share for fresh eating or baking. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
